structure.rationale: The requester supplied a full 7-chapter outline (issue #165), so the chapter order is preserved as the concept order: streaming/why-Kafka, Kafka's own architecture, Avro on its own, the two combined, the schema registry that makes the combination practical, a worked minimal example, then a wrap-up of best practices. Each chapter builds a vocabulary the next chapter assumes, matching the persona's incremental, build-it-a-piece-at-a-time style.
structure.audience: Working programmers new to event streaming and to schema-based serialization — comfortable with code, new to Kafka and Avro specifically.

claims.text: Point-to-point integrations between systems don't scale: every new system that needs the same data means another direct connection, and every format change on one side can break every system wired to it.

Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used to build real-time data pipelines: producers publish events once, and any number of independent consumers can read them, decoupling the systems that produce data from the systems that use it.

A 'data contract' is the agreement about the shape of the data crossing this boundary; without one, a producer can silently change a field's name or type and every downstream consumer breaks at runtime instead of at build time.

pitfalls: Treating 'it's just JSON, we'll figure out the fields as we go' as a data contract — it isn't one until it's enforced somewhere.

claims.text: Producers publish records to Kafka topics; consumers subscribe to topics and read the records, usually as part of a consumer group.
Brokers are the servers that store topic data and serve reads and writes; a Kafka cluster is a set of brokers working together.

A topic is an ordered, durable log of records — the fundamental unit of organization, comparable to a table. A topic is split into partitions so it can be written and read in parallel and scaled across brokers.
Kafka guarantees order within a single partition, not across partitions of the same topic.

Each partition has a designated leader broker that handles all reads and writes for that partition; other brokers hold replicas for fault tolerance, and a leader epoch tracks who is currently in charge as leadership changes.
Within a consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to at most one consumer instance at a time, which is what gives a group parallel processing without two consumers racing over the same records.

Consumer offsets — how far a consumer group has read into each partition — are themselves stored as records in an internal Kafka topic (__consumer_offsets), replicated like any other topic for durability.

pitfalls: Assuming global ordering across a topic — Kafka only orders records within one partition, so events with a causal relationship need the same partition key.
Forgetting that offsets are per consumer group: two different group.id values each read the whole topic from their own position.

claims.text: Serialization is converting an in-memory value into a byte stream for storage or transmission, and deserialization is reversing that.
Avro schemas are written as JSON. A record schema declares type: 'record', a name, an optional namespace, and a fields array; each field has a name, a type, and may declare a default.

Avro defines two encodings: a compact binary encoding (what Kafka and .avro files use in production) and a verbose JSON encoding meant for debugging. In the binary encoding, field names are not written at all — values are positioned purely by the schema's field order, which is what makes it smaller than a self-describing format like JSON.
Because Avro's binary encoding carries no field names or type tags, a binary Avro value cannot be decoded without its schema — unlike JSON, which is self-describing.
An optional field is written as a union with null, e.g. ["null", "string"], and Avro's convention is to list null first so it also serves as that field's implicit default.

snippets.note: Shape matches the Avro 1.11.1 record schema grammar: type/name/namespace/fields, each field with name/type and an optional default.

pitfalls: Forgetting a default on a field you'll ever want to add or drop later — without one, schema evolution across that field breaks (see Schema Registry chapter).
Listing a union's branches in the wrong order — ["string", "null"] is legal but the default (if any) must match the first branch's type, so most schemas put null first.

claims.text: Pairing Kafka with Avro gets you a compact binary payload on the wire (smaller than an equivalent JSON message) plus a schema-checked contract between producers and consumers, instead of an unenforced convention.
Sending the full Avro schema on every single Kafka message would be wasteful — most of the record's bytes would be the schema, repeated on every message, not the data.
The fix is indirection: a central Schema Registry stores each schema once and hands back a small integer schema ID; Kafka messages carry only that ID, not the schema itself.

pitfalls: Trying to solve schema distribution by embedding the schema in every message 'just for now' — it works until message volume makes the overhead visible, and by then it's load-bearing.

claims.text: A Schema Registry is a centralized service that stores every version of every registered schema and validates new registrations against the topic's configured compatibility rule.

Workflow: the producer's Avro serializer registers (or looks up) the schema with the registry, gets back a schema ID, and writes that ID plus the Avro-binary payload to Kafka. It caches the schema-to-ID mapping locally, so it only calls the registry again when the schema actually changes.

The consumer's Avro deserializer reads the schema ID out of the message, fetches (and caches) that exact schema from the registry, and uses it to decode the binary payload — the consumer never needs its own copy of the writer's schema ahead of time.

Compatibility modes govern what schema changes the registry will accept for a subject: BACKWARD (new schema can read data written with the previous schema — the default), FORWARD (old schema can read data written with the new schema), FULL (both directions hold), and *_TRANSITIVE variants that check against every prior version, not just the immediately preceding one.
BACKWARD is the default because it is what lets you rewind a consumer group to the start of a topic and still read every record with the current schema.

pitfalls: Adding a required field with no default — that's a backward-incompatible change under the default compatibility mode, and the registry will reject the registration rather than let it through silently.
Renaming a field instead of adding a new one with an alias — renames read as a drop-and-add pair to the registry and usually fail the compatibility check.

claims.text: A minimal working setup needs a running Kafka broker and a running Schema Registry that the producer and consumer both point at.

A producer using Avro configures its value serializer as the Avro serializer (Confluent's KafkaAvroSerializer is the reference implementation) pointed at the registry URL; the consumer's value deserializer is the matching Avro deserializer, pointed at the same registry.
By default a new consumer only sees messages produced after it starts, so for a first end-to-end test it's simplest to start the consumer before the producer.

snippets.note: The example schema the chapter's producer/consumer pseudo-code sends and reads.

snippets.code:
# Producer (pseudo-code, Confluent-style Avro serializer)
value_serializer = AvroSerializer(schema_registry_client, user_registered_schema)
producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092"})

event = {"userId": "u-42", "email": "ada@example.com", "plan": "pro"}
producer.produce(
    topic="user-registered",
    key=event["userId"],
    value=value_serializer(event, SerializationContext("user-registered", MessageField.VALUE)),
)
producer.flush()
snippets.note: Shape matches the documented Confluent Avro serializer flow: serializer registers/looks up the schema, writes schema-id-prefixed binary Avro.

snippets.code:
# Consumer (pseudo-code, Confluent-style Avro deserializer)
value_deserializer = AvroDeserializer(schema_registry_client)
consumer = Consumer({
    "bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092",
    "group.id": "user-registered-watchers",
    "auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
})
consumer.subscribe(["user-registered"])

while True:
    msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
    if msg is None:
        continue
    event = value_deserializer(msg.value(), SerializationContext("user-registered", MessageField.VALUE))
    handle(event)
snippets.note: Deserializer fetches the writer's schema by the ID embedded in the message; no schema is hardcoded in the consumer.

pitfalls: Pointing the producer and consumer at different Schema Registry instances — schema IDs are only meaningful within the registry that issued them.
Forgetting auto.offset.reset for a brand-new consumer group and being confused when 'nothing arrives' — with no committed offset, the default is to wait for new records only.

claims.text: Kafka moves events; Avro gives those events a compact, typed shape; the Schema Registry is what lets producers and consumers agree on that shape without shipping it on every message.
Version control your schemas the same way you version code — a schema change is an API change to every consumer of that topic.

Pick a compatibility mode deliberately rather than accepting the default everywhere: BACKWARD suits topics where you replay history through new consumers; FORWARD suits topics where old consumers must survive a producer upgrade; FULL is the strictest and safest when both directions matter.

Common pitfalls in production: adding a required field with no default, renaming instead of adding-with-alias, and registering incompatible schemas straight to prod instead of testing compatibility in CI first.
